title: Physics in Real Life — Foundations

competencies.text: Identify how physics concepts improve quality of life in household, health & safety, work productivity, and leisure.

days.title: What Physics Is and Where It Helps
days.content:
🎯 Learning Target

By the end of this week you can explain how physics improves the quality of life in four areas: household, health & safety, work productivity, and leisure.

🔍 What Is Physics?

Physics is the science of matter, energy, motion and force — and how they interact. It answers why things behave the way they do: why a jeepney passenger lurches forward when the driver brakes, why a rice cooker stops boiling at the right time, or why a phone can receive a call from another province.

Engineers, nurses, farmers and athletes use physics every day, even if they never write a formula. When we understand the physics behind a device, we can use it safely, choose better between options, and even improve it.

🧭 Four Areas Where Physics Improves Life

AreaPhysics behind itExample
🏠 HouseholdHeat, electricity, pressureRice cooker, refrigerator, water tank
🏥 Health & safetyForces, light, radiationSeatbelts, eyeglasses, X-ray machines
💼 Work productivityMachines, torque, motorsWheelbarrow, wrench, sewing machine
🎮 LeisureSound, light, wavesSpeakers, cameras, TV and radio

💡 Key Idea

The same concept can serve several areas. Friction keeps you from slipping in the bathroom (safety), lets a bicycle brake (transport) and lets a basketball player stop quickly (leisure). This week we look at each area more closely — one area pair per day.

✅ Quick Check

Answer the 3 questions below. After each answer you will see why it is right or wrong.

scenario.text: A hospital uses an X-ray machine to check whether a patient's arm is broken. Which area of daily life does this MOST directly improve?

choices.label: Health and safety
Household tasks
Work productivity
Leisure and recreation

scenario.explanation: X-rays help doctors see inside the body without surgery, so injuries are found and treated quickly — that is health and safety.

scenario.text: A delivery rider uses a phone map that shows his exact location. Which physics concept makes the phone's GPS work?

choices.label: Electromagnetic (radio) waves
Friction between tires and road
Air pressure in the tires
Sound waves from the horn

scenario.explanation: GPS satellites send radio signals (electromagnetic waves). The phone times these signals to work out its position. Friction, air pressure and sound have nothing to do with locating the phone.

scenario.text: Which example shows physics improving LEISURE?

choices.label: A speaker turning electric signals into sound
A seatbelt holding a passenger in place
A welding machine joining two metal bars
A refrigerator keeping fish cold and fresh

scenario.explanation: Music and entertainment are leisure. The speaker uses vibrations (sound waves). The seatbelt is safety, welding is work productivity, and the refrigerator is household.

days.title: Physics at Home and in Health & Safety
days.content:
🏠 Physics at Home

  • Rice cooker: while there is water in the pot, the temperature stays near 100 °C. When the water is gone, the temperature rises quickly; a temperature sensor (thermostat) detects this and switches the cooker to WARM.
  • Refrigerator: a liquid called the refrigerant absorbs heat from inside as it evaporates, then releases that heat through the coils at the back.
  • Electric fan: a fan does not make air colder. Moving air speeds up the evaporation of sweat and carries heat away from your skin, so you feel cooler.
  • Elevated water tank: water pressure increases with depth, so a tank on the roof gives strong flow to the faucets far below it.

🏥 Physics in Health & Safety

  • Seatbelts, airbags and helmets make your body or head stop more slowly. The longer the stopping time, the smaller the force on you.
  • Eyeglasses use lenses that refract (bend) light so that the image falls exactly on the retina.
  • X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed more by bone, so bones show up clearly on the image.
  • Rubber mats increase friction so feet do not slip on wet tiles.
🤔 Think about it: Why is it more dangerous to jump onto a cement floor than onto a thick mattress from the same height? (Hint: compare the stopping times.)

🔗 Activity 1 — Match the Pairs

Match each physics idea to the household or safety use it explains. When you get a pair right, read the short reason that appears. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

match.why: When the water is used up the pot gets hotter than 100 °C; the sensor detects it and stops the heating.
The refrigerant takes heat from inside as it evaporates and gives it off through the coils at the back.

match.right: Electric fan making you feel cool
match.why: Moving air helps sweat evaporate, which takes heat from your skin. The air itself does not get colder.

match.right: Elevated water tank on the roof
match.why: The deeper a faucet is below the tank, the greater the water pressure, so lower faucets flow strongly.
The airbag makes the head stop over a longer time, so the force on it is much smaller.

match.left: Refraction of light by a lens
match.why: The lens bends light so the image falls exactly on the retina.
Soft tissue lets X-rays through but bone absorbs more, so bones appear clearly.

match.right: Rubber mat on a wet bathroom floor
match.why: The rough rubber increases friction between feet and floor, preventing slips.

days.title: Physics at Work and in Leisure
days.content:
💼 Physics for Work Productivity

Machines let one person do work that would otherwise need many people. Most hand tools use torque — the turning effect of a force:

torque = force × lever arm

Example: pushing a wrench with 20 N at 0.10 m from the bolt gives 2 N·m of torque. Pushing with the same 20 N at 0.30 m gives 6 N·m — three times the turning effect. That is why a longer crowbar or wrench works better.

  • Wheelbarrow: a lever — the load sits between the wheel and your hands, so a small lifting force supports a heavy load.
  • Ramp (inclined plane): you push with less force over a longer distance instead of lifting straight up.
  • Electric motors in sewing machines and drills change electrical energy into motion.

🎮 Physics in Leisure

  • Sound is a mechanical wave: it needs air (or another material) to travel. Speakers vibrate to make these waves.
  • Radio and TV signals are electromagnetic waves: they travel through air and even empty space, so no cable is needed.
  • Cameras use lenses that refract light to form a sharp image.
  • In sports, friction between shoes and the court lets players start and stop quickly.

🎯 Activity 2 — Scenario Challenge

Each scenario asks you to apply or judge a physics idea in a real situation. Read all choices — they are similar on purpose. After each answer, read the explanation. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

scenario.text: Tita Liza says, "Leave the electric fan on in the empty bedroom so the room will be cooler when we come back." Is she right?

choices.label: No — it cools skin by evaporation; the air does not get colder
Yes — the spinning blades change electric energy into cold air
Yes — the moving air carries the heat out through the walls
No — a fan works only if the room is already air-conditioned

scenario.explanation: A fan cools PEOPLE: moving air speeds up the evaporation of sweat and carries heat from the skin. Its motor even adds a little heat. With nobody in the room, the fan only wastes electricity.

scenario.text: Mang Ben cannot pull out a rusty nail with a short claw hammer. Which change will MOST likely help him?

choices.label: Use a longer bar and push at the far end of the handle
Use a heavier hammer and push near the hammer's head
Pull faster but grip the handle closer to the nail
Wet the nail with water so that it slides out easily

scenario.explanation: Torque = force × lever arm. A longer bar pushed at its far end gives a bigger lever arm, so the same effort produces more turning effect. Gripping near the head or the nail SHORTENS the lever arm.

scenario.text: Helmet X has a thick foam lining; Helmet Y has a thin, hard plastic lining. Which better protects the head in a fall, and why?

choices.label: X, because the foam makes the head stop more slowly
Y, because hard plastic does not bend when it is hit
Y, because a thinner lining makes the helmet lighter
X, because the foam makes the head bounce off quickly

scenario.explanation: The foam crushes during impact, so the head stops over a LONGER time. A longer stopping time means a smaller force on the skull. A hard lining stops the head almost instantly — a larger force.

scenario.text: During a typhoon the town's cable TV line is cut, but a battery-powered radio still gets news from Manila. What allows the radio to receive the broadcast?

choices.label: Radio waves that travel through air and empty space
Sound waves from the station that travel all the way
Electric current that flows through the wet ground
Light from the station that reflects off the clouds

scenario.explanation: Broadcasts are carried by electromagnetic (radio) waves, which need no cable and can travel very far. Sound waves fade quickly and could never travel from Manila to the town.

scenario.text: A water tank sits on the roof of a 3-storey house. Which faucet will have the STRONGEST flow?

choices.label: The ground-floor faucet, farthest below the tank
The third-floor faucet, closest to the tank
All faucets flow equally, since they share one tank
The faucet with the widest pipe, on any floor

scenario.explanation: Water pressure increases with depth — with the height of water above the faucet. The ground-floor faucet has the tallest column of water above it, so it has the highest pressure and strongest flow.

days.title: Thinking Like a Physicist
days.content:
🧠 Thinking Like a Physicist

Knowing the names of concepts is not enough. A physicist uses them to explain and to decide. Use these four steps whenever you meet a claim or a problem:

  1. Observe — What exactly happens? (Who, what, how fast, how strong?)
  2. Identify the concept — friction? pressure? torque? stopping time? waves?
  3. Explain with the concept — connect cause and effect in one or two sentences.
  4. Evaluate — Is the claim correct? Which option is safer, cheaper or more effective?

📝 Worked Example

Claim: "Leave the electric fan on in the empty bedroom so the room will be cool when we come back."

  • Observe: nobody is in the room; the fan only moves air.
  • Identify: a fan cools people by speeding up evaporation of sweat; its motor actually gives off a little heat.
  • Explain: with no one inside, there is no sweat to evaporate, so the air does not get colder.
  • Evaluate: the claim is wrong; turning the fan off saves electricity.

Notice that the best answer is not the one with the most "science words" — it is the one where the concept truly explains what happens.

🔐 Formative Check — Escape the Lab

You have 3 lives and 6 keys. Each correct answer earns a key; each wrong answer costs a life. You need 70% (5 of 6) to complete the week. Read the explanation after every question.

escape.text: A tailor replaces her foot-pedal sewing machine with one that has an electric motor. Which area of daily life is MOST improved?

choices.label: Work productivity
Health and safety
Leisure and recreation
Food preservation

escape.explanation: The motor lets her sew faster with less effort — more output in less time. That is work productivity.

escape.text: A wheelbarrow lets one worker move a heavy load of sand. What does it mainly do?

choices.label: It works as a lever, so less effort is needed
It removes most of the weight of the sand load
It changes the sand into a lighter material
It makes gravity pull less hard near the wheel

escape.explanation: The wheelbarrow is a lever: the load sits between the wheel (fulcrum) and your hands, so a small effort supports a large load. The sand's weight and gravity do not change.

escape.text: A softball player pulls her glove backward while catching a fast ball. Why does this hurt less?

choices.label: The ball stops over a longer time
The ball stops over a shorter time
The ball loses some of its mass
Gravity pulls the ball to one side

escape.explanation: Moving the glove back makes the ball stop over a longer time, so the force on her hand is smaller — the same idea as seatbelts and airbags.

escape.text: Which of these is NOT an example of physics improving health and safety?

choices.label: A television showing a cartoon
A helmet lining that crushes on impact
A thermometer reading body temperature
Eyeglasses that focus light correctly

escape.explanation: A TV show is leisure. Helmets (stopping time), thermometers (heat and temperature) and eyeglasses (refraction) all protect health or safety.

escape.text: A friend says, "Seatbelts are useless — you can just hold on to the seat in a crash." Which reply is BEST supported by physics?

choices.label: Your arms cannot supply the huge force needed in a sudden stop
Seatbelts only work when the vehicle is moving very slowly
Holding on is better, because seatbelts add to your body weight
Seatbelts protect only the driver, not the other passengers

escape.explanation: In a sudden stop your body keeps moving because of inertia. Stopping it quickly needs a force far larger than your arms can give. The belt holds you and spreads the force across your body.

escape.text: Your video call freezes whenever you go into a room with thick concrete walls. Which explanation fits physics BEST?

choices.label: The thick walls absorb and block part of the radio signal
The concrete walls slow down the sound of your own voice
The phone's screen reflects too much of the indoor light
The still air inside the room is unable to carry the signal

escape.explanation: Phones send and receive radio (electromagnetic) waves. Thick concrete absorbs part of these waves, so the signal gets weak. Radio waves do not need moving air, and screen light is unrelated.
